nameStory: American trumpet vine gets its name from its spectacular trumpet-shaped flowers that flare out like miniature brass instruments. The blooms are so perfectly shaped that they look like nature's own orchestra waiting for a tiny musician to play them! Native Americans and early settlers noticed how these bright orange-red trumpets seemed to call out to hummingbirds from across the garden.
description: American trumpet vine is a vigorous, deciduous woody vine that can climb up to 33 feet high using aerial rootlets that grip onto bark, fences, or buildings. It produces clusters of stunning orange-red trumpet-shaped flowers that are about 3 inches long and flare open at the mouth. The vine has compound leaves made up of 7-11 leaflets arranged in pairs, creating a lush, tropical-looking canopy. This native climber is beloved by hummingbirds and butterflies but can be quite aggressive in spreading through underground roots.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant orange-red trumpet-shaped blooms, about 3 inches long, clustered at branch tips. The flowers feel waxy and sturdy, with five lobes that flare out dramatically from a narrow tube - perfect landing pads for hummingbirds.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-11 oval leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem, plus one terminal leaflet. Each leaflet is 2-4 inches long with serrated edges and feels smooth on top but slightly fuzzy underneath.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Aggressive climbing vine that attaches to surfaces using small aerial rootlets that feel rough and wiry. Young stems are green and flexible, while older stems develop brown, fibrous bark that can be surprisingly thick.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, bean-like seed pods (4-6 inches) that split open to release flat, papery seeds with transparent wings. The pods start green and turn brown, often persisting through winter with a dry, rattling sound when shaken.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature stems develop stringy, fibrous bark that peels in long strips. The bark feels rough and shreddy, quite different from the smooth green stems of young growth.

habitat: American trumpet vine thrives in woodland edges, riverbanks, and disturbed areas with rich, moist soil and partial to full sun. In New England, look for it climbing trees along streams, sprawling over stone walls, or covering abandoned structures in old farmsteads. It's equally happy in cultivated gardens where it can quickly take over trellises, fences, and even climb up house walls if not carefully managed.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in spring, unfolding as bronzy-green compound leaflets. The vine puts on rapid growth during late spring, sending out long, flexible shoots that can grow several feet in just weeks.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from July through August, when clusters of orange-red trumpet flowers create a spectacular display. This is when the vine is most easily identified and when hummingbirds are constantly visiting.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-green before dropping, and the distinctive long seed pods ripen from green to brown. Seeds with papery wings disperse on autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: Bare woody stems show the vine's climbing structure, with distinctive aerial rootlets visible on surfaces. Brown seed pods often persist, rattling in winter winds and providing identification clues.

funFact: Trumpet vine flowers are perfectly designed hummingbird restaurants - the nectar is stored so deep in the trumpet that only hummingbirds' long tongues can reach it, and the flower's sturdy construction can actually support the weight of these tiny birds as they hover and feed!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with cross vine (Bignonia capreolata), another trumpet-flowered climber, but cross vine has only 2 leaflets per compound leaf instead of 7-11, and its flowers are more yellow-orange. Remember: 'American trumpet has MANY leaflets, cross vine has just a CROSS of two.'
contextualKnowledge: Also called 'cow-itch vine' because the sap can cause skin irritation in sensitive people, similar to poison ivy. Despite being a beloved native plant that supports hummingbirds, it's considered invasive in some areas due to its aggressive spreading through underground runners - a classic case of 'right plant, wrong place' when it escapes cultivation.
compareHints: American trumpet vine is the only Campsis species commonly found in New England. Within the broader trumpet vine family (Bignoniaceae), it's distinguished from cross vine by its many-leafleted compound leaves versus cross vine's simple two-leaflet arrangement. The orange-red color is also more intense than the yellower trumpets of cross vine, and American trumpet vine's climbing habit using aerial rootlets differs from cross vine's tendril-climbing method.
